claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in structural materials for fusion plasma-facing components is governed by the formation and evolution of coherent nanoprecipitates.
High-temperature toughness in structural materials for fusion plasma-facing components is governed by the formation and evolution of coherent nanoprecipitates.
Coherent nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion through obstacle hardening.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances resistance to plastic deformation.
Obstacle hardening by coherent nanoprecipitates enhances plastic strain.
Obstacle hardening by coherent nanoprecipitates improves toughness.
The initial high-temperature material state above 500°C has a uniform distribution of solute atoms.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can be introduced in a stepwise controllable manner through a combination of experimental and simulation approaches.
Temperatures above 500°C and high applied stresses mimic the fusion plasma environment relevant to the proposed materials.
Introducing coherent nanoprecipitates will produce a 20% increase in plastic strain relative to material without nanoprecipitates.
Introducing coherent nanoprecipitates will produce a 30% increase in toughness relative to material without nanoprecipitates.
The hypothesized mechanism applies from 500°C to 1000°C.
The hypothesized mechanism applies at stress levels up to 500 MPa.
Nanoprecipitate size and distribution may influence the predicted response.
Interactions between nanoprecipitates and other microstructural features may influence the predicted response.
The hypothesis is falsified if the nanoprecipitate-containing material shows less than a 10% increase in plastic strain and less than a 20% increase in toughness relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The precipitates are said to increase resistance to plastic deformation while also increasing plastic strain. The hypothesis does not distinguish strength, creep strain, strain to failure, or another strain metric, leaving the predicted direction internally ambiguous.

The prediction specifies 20% greater plastic strain and 30% greater toughness, but falsification requires both gains to fall below separate lower thresholds. Thus, failure of either principal prediction alone would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated conjunctive rule.
